newsitem.title: UK: UK minimum wage need not mean job losses -study.
newsitem.headline: UK minimum wage need not mean job losses -study.

text.p: A national minimum wage in Britain could have adverse effects on jobs if it was set at the level proposed by trade unions, but a lower level might actually boost employment, according to a study by the Centre for Economic Performance (CEP).

The study, to be published on Friday, said a minimum hourly wage of 4.40 stg (equivalent in 1996 terms to the 4.26 stg figure recently adopted by the Trades Union Congress) would cover around five million employees and cost three percent of the national wage bill to introduce.
"Such a rate would run the risk of adverse employment effects," authors Sue Fernie and David Metcalf concluded.

The opposition Labour party, which is well ahead of the ruling Conservatives in opinion polls, is committed to introducing a minimum wage if it wins a general election due by May 1997, but it has not specified what the level would be.

The study said that if the minimum wage was set at 3.20 stg -- the 1996 equivalent of the average basic rate set by Britain's wages councils at the time of their abolition in 1993 -- there would probably not be adverse effects on jobs.
"Indeed, such a rate around 3.20 stg may even boost employment by giving an incentive to take jobs previously on offer below 3.20 stg," it said.
Setting the wage at around 3.70 stg, around half median male hourly earnings, might cause job losses in sectors such as catering and retailing.
The CEP said research on the effects of a minimum wage on employment was inconclusive.
Studies suggested the work of wages councils had been detrimental to jobs in the 1960s and 1970s but was neutral or even beneficial to employment after 1980.

"The evidence that the 1993 abolition of the councils gave no boost to jobs also implies that a national minimum wage set at the previous council rate, suitably uprated to the present, would be unlikely to cost jobs," the CEP said.

The study said a national minimum wage would, by itself, have a very modest impact on poverty. "The poorest families are those headed by the long term unemployed, lone parents or a low earner with lots of children," it said.
But it would almost certainly reduce wage inequality.

"Wage inequality is now greater than at any time in the last century, so a national minimum wage can be viewed as a mechanism to offset some of the growth in inequality that has occurred since 1980," the study said.
